child-development-milestones-ages-2-to-4:
These two years contain more change than any other stretch of childhood except the first. Language arrives in a rush, the body becomes reliable, and somewhere in the middle of it a person appears who has opinions and will tell you about them.

What follows is what is typically happening, not a list to check off. Every age here is the middle of a wide range.

Language

At two, most children have a few dozen words and are starting to put two together. By four they are holding conversations, asking constant questions, using past tense, and telling you about something that happened yesterday, which is a bigger cognitive leap than it sounds because it requires holding an event in mind and rebuilding it in words for somebody who was not there.

The vocabulary growth in this window is steep, and it tracks closely with how much a child is spoken to. Not how much they are taught, how much they are talked with.

The body

Walking becomes running, then climbing, then jumping with both feet. Stairs go from one-foot-per-step to alternating. Hands get more precise: scribbles become circles, then a face with something like features. Most children can use a spoon reliably, then a fork, and are trying zips and buttons.

A great deal of what looks like restlessness is a body that needs to move to develop. It is not a behaviour problem and it does not respond to being asked to stop.

The will

This is what the two-year-old reputation is about, and it is worth reframing. A child this age is discovering that they are a separate person with separate wants, which is a developmental achievement rather than a decline in behaviour. The refusals, the strong preferences, the sudden fury when a banana is broken: all of it is a will arriving before any capacity to manage it exists.

Self-control at this age is almost entirely borrowed from you. There is very little internal machinery yet, which is why a calm adult shortens a tantrum and a matching one extends it.

Play and other children

At two, mostly alongside rather than with. Sharing is not really available and asking for it repeatedly does not accelerate it. By three and four, pretend play takes over, roles get assigned and negotiated, and the first real friendships appear. This is when children start playing games with rules they invent and then argue about, which is worth more developmentally than it looks.

What is worth mentioning to someone

Not a single late thing. Worth raising: no words by around eighteen months or no two-word phrases by around two and a half, losing a skill they had, no interest in other people, no pretend play by three, or your own steady unease across months.

This piece is general guidance and is not a substitute for an assessment by someone who knows your child.
child-development-milestones-ages-4-to-6:
This is the stretch where a child becomes recognisably a person who could manage a morning without you. It is also where the gap between children is at its widest and least meaningful, because school entry lines up children of very different developmental ages and invites comparison between them.

Thinking

Imagination is at full strength: elaborate pretend worlds, invisible friends, long stories with a plot that mostly holds. Children this age can sort, sequence and classify, and they begin asking why about causes rather than about names. They still reason from what things look like rather than what they must be, which is why a tall thin glass obviously holds more than a short wide one.

Language

Grammar largely arrives. Sentences get longer and more complex, jokes and wordplay appear, and a child can retell an event in order. Sound awareness develops in this window: hearing rhyme, hearing that words start the same, clapping syllables. That is the foundation reading will later be built on, and it happens entirely by ear.

Feelings

The first real self-control appears and is fragile. A five-year-old can wait, take a turn and stop themselves some of the time, and loses all of it when tired. They begin naming feelings, which is the first step towards managing them. They also begin comparing themselves to other children, which is where confidence starts to be built or dented.

Friendships

Play becomes genuinely cooperative. Children this age negotiate roles, fall out, and mostly repair without help, which is the practice that matters. Preferences for particular friends appear. Fairness becomes an intense concern and is applied inconsistently, usually in their own favour.

The body

Hopping, skipping, catching, pedalling, climbing with confidence. Hands become capable of scissors, threading, buttons and laces. Most children can dress themselves by six, if they have been allowed to practise rather than dressed for speed.

What this window is really for

Not academics. The things developing here are the ones later academics sit on: sustained attention, hearing the parts inside words, the capacity to wait, and the confidence to try something that might not work. A child strong in those arrives at school work in better shape than one who was taught letters early and is anxious.

Worth mentioning to someone: speech that others cannot understand, no interest in other children, unusual difficulty with everyday transitions, or your own persistent unease over months.
child-development-milestones-ages-6-to-8:
Six to eight is when childhood gets its second face. Reading steadies, rules start to matter enormously, and a child begins measuring themselves against everyone around them. It is also, for most families, the first age where a child's inner life is genuinely private.

What arrives

Reading becomes usable. For most children decoding stops being the main event somewhere in here, and reading turns into a way of finding things out rather than a task. The shift to watch for is not accuracy but effort: reading correctly while concentrating hard is not the same as reading fluently enough to think about the meaning.

Logic, of a concrete kind. They can reason about real things reliably: that a quantity does not change when you pour it into a different glass, that events have causes, that a rule applies even when nobody is watching. Abstract reasoning is still some way off.

Real friendship. Not just playmates. Children this age have preferences, loyalties and fallings-out that matter to them, and the social world starts to occupy real attention.

Competence as identity. This is the big one. A child this age is working out what they are good at, and the answer becomes part of who they think they are. Finished work matters more than it did; so does being seen to manage something without help.

What is still hard, and will be for years

Holding several instructions. Working memory is still small. The child who goes upstairs and returns with nothing is not being difficult.

Losing. Games matter now, which makes losing them worse. The capacity to lose well is built slowly across this whole stretch.

Managing frustration alone. Better than at four, nowhere near adult. A hard piece of homework still needs a person nearby more than it needs advice.

Time. Planning backwards from a deadline is barely available. So is any accurate sense of how long something will take.

The comparison problem

Because children this age are actively deciding what they are good at, this is when a casual comparison does the most damage. A child who concludes at seven that they are not a maths person will hold that for a decade, and it will be more limiting than any actual gap in ability.

The useful counter is specific noticing. Naming what they did rather than what they are: that they kept going, that they tried it a second way, that they finished something difficult.

What helps most here

Volume of easy reading. Real responsibility they can actually complete. Time with friends without adults arranging it. Something they are allowed to get good at slowly. And an adult who is steady when work is hard, rather than one who takes over.

Worth raising with someone who can observe directly: reading that has not clicked after a year of instruction, difficulty across settings that has lasted months, or a child who has stopped wanting to try.
how-to-support-your-childs-development-a:
Ranked by how much difference they make, not by how impressive they sound. The first four are worth more than everything sold to parents put together, and none of them cost anything.

  1. Talk with them, constantly and about real things. Not teaching, conversation. Narrate what you are doing, ask questions you do not know the answer to, and leave silences long enough for a slow answer. Vocabulary and background knowledge are built here, and between them they set the ceiling on reading comprehension years later.

  2. Protect sleep. It is the single largest variable in how a child functions, and short sleep presents as inattention, silliness and a short fuse rather than as tiredness. Fixing sleep improves attention, mood and self-control at once, which no activity does.

  3. Read aloud, above their level, for years longer than feels necessary. Keep going after they can read alone. Read-aloud carries sentence structures and words their own reading cannot reach yet.

  4. Leave long unstructured stretches. Deep self-chosen play is where attention, negotiation and self-control are practised voluntarily. This means resisting the urge to fill the day, and tolerating the boredom that comes before invention.

  5. Let them do things badly. Pouring, dressing, carrying, cutting, paying. Every task an adult does for speed is practice a child does not get. Competence is built out of being allowed to be slow and clumsy at something real.

  6. Get outside. Distance vision, whole-body movement, risk calibration and unsupervised negotiation are all things indoors cannot provide.

  7. Eat together where you can. It is one of the few reliably measured family practices, and most of its value is probably the conversation rather than the food.

  8. Give them a real job. Something the household actually depends on, at their level, that nobody redoes afterwards. Responsibility is the experience of something depending on you, and it cannot be simulated.

What to stop worrying about

Whether they know their letters before school. Whether the activities are educational. Whether other children are ahead. Enrichment classes, unless the child loves the thing. Screen minutes, if sleep, movement, conversation and outdoor time are all intact, because then it is genuinely a smaller factor than the discourse suggests.

The thing underneath all of it

A child develops best in an environment that is predictable, responsive and unhurried. Predictable so they are not spending attention on what happens next. Responsive so their attempts to communicate get answered. Unhurried so there is room to try things slowly.

None of that is a programme. It is a household, run in a particular way, and it is what the research keeps pointing at when it is not being sold anything.
